summary:
Dagestan stands under the national framework of Russia, where the risks facing transgender and LGBT visitors have sharpened markedly since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these statutes face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and the United States State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The same laws operate inside Dagestan as they do in every other Russian region.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) names the North Caucasus, including Dagestan, as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and North Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024 that involved abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings, and it assesses transgender people and visible advocates as a defined category within that finding.

Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia. Its advisory warns of violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons and singles out the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan. It also flags frequent terrorist attacks in Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and Stavropol Krai, and states that entry to certain areas and regions requires special permission from the Ministry of the Interior.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, who works in exile, told the Human Rights House Foundation that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He said the situation worsens year on year.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume nationally has risen alongside severity. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda statutes have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those laws brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two further venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and the Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented well beyond the North Caucasus. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

Dagestan is one of four territories named in the Canadian advisory for frequent terrorist attacks, a security condition distinct from, and additional to, the anti-LGBT enforcement described above. Comparable persecution findings in the region have repeatedly centred on Chechnya, which provides the documented template for the campaigns the Home Office attributes to Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024.
localsOnly:
The bans on legal gender recognition and on gender-affirming care apply to residents of Dagestan as they do to visitors, leaving no lawful domestic route to change gender markers on official documents or to obtain transition-related medical care. The extremist designation exposes residents to administrative and criminal charges for displaying alleged symbols or for alleged participation, the charge category in which Human Rights Watch counted 101 convictions nationally by 30 June 2025.

Residents, as well as visitors, are exposed to the coercion documented by North Caucasus SOS: David Isteev's account to the Human Rights House Foundation holds that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, and that the pattern worsens annually. The Home Office note records abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities across the 2017 to 2024 period, with transgender people and visible advocates assessed specifically.

The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. That finding provides the basis on which a resident of Dagestan fleeing persecution would be assessed by the UK asylum system.
outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced in the current inventory: any count of prosecutions, raids, deaths or abductions recorded inside Dagestan itself between 2017 and 2024. The Home Office finding for the North Caucasus is stated at regional level and is not broken down by republic in the material available here.

Unresolved: whether the Ministry of the Interior special-permission requirement identified in the Canadian advisory applies to ordinary tourist or short-stay entry to Dagestan, or only to designated localities within it. The advisory excerpt does not specify which areas and regions the requirement covers.

Unresolved: the current posture of Dagestan's own interior and security bodies toward the 2023 extremism and propaganda provisions. No Dagestan-specific enforcement reporting, sentence figures or raid records were available for this pass.

Source dating note: the UK Home Office country policy note carries a June 2025 publication date with a page update recorded on 12 August 2026, so individual passages may have been revised after initial publication. Verification against the current live version remains outstanding.
